entry: Type of [[Lawyer|lawyer]] in [[Common law|common law]] jurisdictions, specializing in courtroom advocacy and litigation. Barristers originated in the Inns of Court of the medieval English legal system and are distinguished from solicitors, who generally have more direct access to clients. In [[England]] and Wales, barristers may seek authorization from the Bar Standards Board to conduct litigation. In the United States, the distinction between barristers and attorneys-at-law does not exist.

American politician and major general in the Air Force Reserve. A [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] senator from Arizona in 1953–65 and 1969–87, he was the party's presidential nominee in 1964, losing in a landslide to incumbent [[Lyndon B. Johnson]]. In 1974 he and representatives John Jacob Rhodes and Hugh Scott urged [[Richard Nixon]] to resign as evidence of a cover-up in the [[Watergate scandal]] became overwhelming. Many pundits and historians believe he laid the foundation for the conservative movement that helped bring about the presidency of [[Ronald Reagan]].

American singer, songwriter and record producer. His hits include "Mandy" and "Could It Be Magic." He has recorded 51 Top 40 singles on the Adult Contemporary chart, 13 of which reached number one, and has sold more than 85 million records as a solo artist worldwide. He has also written songs for commercials for corporations such as [[McDonald's]] and [[Pepsi|Pepsi Cola]], and produced albums for [[Bette Midler]] and [[Dionne Warwick]].

American R&B, [[Soul music|soul]] and [[Disco|disco]] singer, songwriter and record producer. A two-time [[Grammy Awards|Grammy Award]] winner known for his bass voice, he had his greatest success in the 1970s as a solo singer and with the Love Unlimited Orchestra, which made the number-one hit "Love's Theme," written by White. He recorded 20 studio albums and had 20 gold and 10 platinum singles, with worldwide record sales in excess of 100 million.

Spanish Dominican friar, historian and social reformer. Las Casas arrived in [[Hispaniola]] as one of the first Spanish settlers in the Americas and initially held Indigenous laborers under the encomienda system. In 1515 he gave up his laborers and encomienda and advocated before Charles V for the rights of Natives. He later entered the Dominican order and worked as a missionary among the Maya of [[Guatemala]]. The New Laws of 1542 were an important victory for his lobbying. At the Valladolid debate in 1550 he argued that Indigenous peoples were fully human. His *A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies* described the atrocities committed against them. Early in his career he had advocated African slaves to replace Indigenous labor, but he later regarded all forms of slavery as equally wrong. After his death he was widely venerated, which led to the opening of his cause for beatification in the [[Catholic Church]].

Philosopher of Portuguese-Jewish origin who lived in the Dutch Republic. He was born in [[Amsterdam]] and was expelled from his Jewish community in 1656 after challenging rabbinic authority and Jewish doctrines. He then supported himself by grinding lenses and devoted himself to philosophy. Influenced by [[Stoicism]], Thomas Hobbes and [[René Descartes|Descartes]], he was a leading philosopher of the [[Dutch Golden Age]]. His *Tractatus Theologico-Politicus* questioned the divine origin of the [[Hebrew Bible]] and argued that ecclesiastical authority should have no role in a secular, democratic state. In his *Ethics*, he equates [[God]] with nature; scholars interpret this view variously as pantheistic, panentheistic or atheistic. His works, published posthumously by friends, influenced philosophers for the next two centuries.

Center of mass around which two or more bodies orbit. A barycenter is a dynamical point rather than a physical object and is important in [[Astronomy|astronomy]] and [[Astrophysics|astrophysics]]. If one body is much more massive than the other and they are close together, the barycenter lies within the more massive body, which appears to wobble rather than orbit. For the [[Earth]]–[[Moon]] system, it lies on average 4,671 km (2,902 mi) from Earth's center, which is 74% of Earth's radius of 6,378 km (3,963 mi). For bodies of similar mass, such as [[Pluto]] and its satellite [[Charon (moon)|Charon]], the barycenter lies between them. Owing to the large distance between [[Jupiter]] and the [[Sun]], their barycenter lies slightly outside the Sun, although the Sun is a thousandfold more massive.

Type of [[Hadron|hadron]] (subatomic particle) composed of three [[Quark|quarks]]. Baryons are [[Fermion|fermions]] with half-integer spin. The [[Proton]] and [[Neutron]] are the most familiar baryons, and they make up most of the mass of visible matter in the universe. The name, introduced by Abraham Pais, comes from the Greek *barýs*, meaning heavy, because most known elementary particles were lighter than baryons when the term was coined. Exotic baryons containing five quarks, called pentaquarks, have also been discovered. A census of the universe's baryons indicates that 10% could be found inside galaxies, 50% to 60% in the circumgalactic medium, and 30% to 40% in the warm–hot intergalactic medium.

Group of subcortical nuclei found in the brains of [[Vertebrate|vertebrates]]. The basal ganglia are involved in regulating voluntary movement, procedural learning, habit formation, eye movements, cognition and emotion. Their main components include the striatum, the globus pallidus and the substantia nigra, which is the source of striatal [[Dopamine|dopamine]]. Their dysfunction results in movement disorders such as [[Parkinson's disease]] and [[Huntington's disease]], and in behavioral conditions including [[Tourette syndrome]] and [[Obsessive–compulsive disorder]].

Fine-grained extrusive [[Igneous rock|igneous rock]] rich in [[Magnesium]] and [[Iron]]. Basalt forms when low-viscosity [[Lava]] cools rapidly at or near the surface of a rocky planet or moon. More than 90% of all volcanic rock on Earth is basalt, and geologists observe basalt lava erupting at about 20 volcanoes per year. Its silica content of between 45% and 52% gives basalt lava a low viscosity, so flows spread over great areas. Flood basalts, thick sequences of such flows, can cover hundreds of thousands of square kilometers. The plains of [[Venus]], which cover about 80% of its surface, are basaltic, and basalt is also common on [[Mars]].

[[India|Indian]] philosopher, poet and social reformer of the Shiva-focused bhakti movement. His influence peaked during the reign of King Bijjala II in Karnataka, where as chief minister he used the state treasury to fund social reforms. He spread social awareness through vachanas, poems in [[Kannada]], and rejected gender and social discrimination, superstitions and rituals. He introduced the ishtalinga necklace, to be worn by every person regardless of birth as a reminder of devotion to [[Shiva]]. He also launched the Anubhava Mantapa, a public assembly that drew men and women from many walks of life to discuss spiritual and social issues. Traditional legends credit him as the founder of the Lingayats, but modern scholarship holds that he revived, refined and energized an existing tradition. Scholars note that poems and legends about him were written down long after his death, which raises questions about their accuracy.

Bat-and-ball game between two teams of nine players each, who take turns batting and fielding. Batters advance around four bases to score runs, and the team with the most runs after a defined number of innings wins. Baseball evolved from older bat-and-ball games popular in [[England]] in the mid-18th century and developed into organized clubs in [[North America]] by the mid-19th century. It has been unofficially recognized as the national sport of the [[United States]] since the late 19th century, although it is less popular there than some other sports. Playoffs in [[Major League Baseball|Major League Baseball (MLB)]] culminate in the [[World Series]]. Baseball was played at the Olympic Games from 1992 to 2008 and in 2020, and will return in 2028.

City in northwestern [[Switzerland]] on the [[Rhine]] River. Basel has 177,595 inhabitants within its municipal limits and is Switzerland's third most populous city. It is commonly considered the cultural capital of Switzerland, and its Kunstmuseum (1661) was the first collection of art accessible to the public in the world. The University of Basel, founded in 1460, is the country's oldest university. The city is home to Art Basel and to the headquarters of the Bank for International Settlements.

Breed of hunting dog originating in [[Central Africa]], including the [[Republic of the Congo]]. The Fédération Cynologique Internationale places it in the [[Spitz]] and "primitive types" categories, while the American Kennel Club classifies it as a [[Hound|hound]]. Its unusually shaped larynx produces a yodel-like "talking" sound rather than a bark, earning it the nickname "barkless" dog. Egyptian murals as old as 4,500 years depict dogs with curled tails and erect ears that have been identified with the breed.

Syrian physician and military officer who was president of [[Syria]] from 2000 until his overthrow in 2024. He succeeded his father, Hafez al-Assad, who had ruled from 1970 to 2000. After protests began in 2011, his government's crackdown led to the [[Syrian civil war]]. He fled to [[Moscow]] in December 2024 as rebel forces entered [[Damascus]], and Russia granted him political asylum. In August 2026 a Syrian court convicted him *in absentia* of [[War crime|war crimes]] and crimes against humanity and sentenced him to death.

Republic of [[Russia]] (pop., 2025: 4,046,094) between the [[Volga|Volga River]] and the [[Ural Mountains]] in Eastern Europe. Its capital and largest city is [[Ufa]]. It is the most populous republic of Russia and borders [[Tatarstan]] to the west. The name, literally "land of the Bashkirs," derives from the Bashkir ethnic group. The republic was established in 1917 and in 1919 became the Bashkir ASSR, the first autonomous republic in the Russian SFSR. On October 11, 1990, it adopted a Declaration of State Sovereignty. Its population is multiethnic, including significant proportions of Russians, Bashkirs and Tatars, with urban dwellers forming the majority. Its economy relies heavily on oil extraction and processing.

Division of fungi that, with [[Ascomycota]], forms the subkingdom Dikarya, often called the higher fungi. Members, called basidiomycetes, reproduce sexually on club-shaped basidia that usually bear four external spores called basidiospores. The division includes agarics, puffballs, bracket fungi, boletes, chanterelles, smuts and rusts, as well as [[Mushroom|mushrooms]] and [[Yeast|yeasts]] such as Cryptococcus, the human pathogenic yeast. Many species are decomposers of wood, and many form mutualistic associations with plant roots. A distinctive feature, the clamp connection, helps identify members of the division. Traditionally it was divided into two classes, now obsolete: the homobasidiomycetes, including true mushrooms, and the heterobasidiomycetes, including the jelly, rust and smut fungi.

Culinary [[Herb|herb]] (*Ocimum basilicum*) of the family [[Lamiaceae]], also called great basil. Native to tropical and subtropical Asia and Australasia, from [[India]] and [[Sri Lanka]] east to southeastern China, [[Taiwan]] and [[Southeast Asia]], it is used in [[Cuisine|cuisines]] worldwide. In temperate climates it is treated as an annual, though it can be a short-lived perennial in warmer regions. Plants reach between 30 and 150 centimeters (1 and 5 feet) in height, with glossy leaves arranged in opposite pairs on square stems. In Western cuisine the term usually refers to sweet basil, also called Genovese basil. The essential oil of European basil contains linalool and methyl chavicol (estragole) in a ratio of about 3:1.

[[Byzantine Empire|Byzantine]] emperor (r. 976–1025), given the epithet the Bulgar-Slayer. Basil and his brother Constantine VIII were crowned as children, but generals held power until Basil became senior emperor in 976. His reign of 49 years and 11 months was the longest of any [[Roman emperor]]. After civil wars against powerful Anatolian generals ended in 989, he oversaw the expansion of the eastern frontier and the subjugation of the [[First Bulgarian Empire]]. A campaign against the Khazar Khaganate gained part of [[Crimea]], and he led successful campaigns against the Kingdom of Georgia. His sister Anna's marriage to Vladimir I of Kiev, offered in exchange for military support, led to the Christianization of [[Kievan Rus'|Kievan Rus']]. He is regarded as a Greek national hero, though he is despised among Bulgarians.

Early Christian bishop and theologian in [[Cappadocia]], known as Saint Basil the Great. He served as bishop of Caesarea Mazaca from 370 until his death. He supported the [[Nicene Creed]] and opposed heresies such as [[Arianism]] and Apollinarianism. His most enduring legacy is the Basileias, believed to be one of the earliest Christian hospitals for the poor. He established guidelines for monastic life focusing on community life, liturgical prayer and manual labor. With his brother [[Gregory of Nyssa]] and friend [[Gregory of Nazianzus]], he is one of the Cappadocian Fathers. He is considered a saint in both Eastern and Western Christianity, and the [[Eastern Orthodox Church]] and Eastern Catholic Churches give him the title Great Hierarch.

[[Weaving|Weaving]] or sewing of pliable materials, such as [[Fiber|fiber]], [[Bark (botany)|bark]] or [[Willow|willow]], into objects such as baskets, mats and mesh bags, or even furniture. Basketry is one of the most widespread crafts in human history, although natural materials decay, so evidence is limited. The most common evidence is weave imprints on fragments of [[Pottery|clay pots]]. The oldest known baskets, from Faiyum in [[Egypt]], have been carbon dated to between 10,000 and 12,000 years old, and the oldest complete basket, from the Negev, dates to 10,500 years old. During the [[Industrial Revolution]], baskets were used in factories and for packing, and wicker furniture became fashionable in Victorian society. Basketry is classified into four types: coiled, plaiting, twining, and wicker and splint. Many [[Indigenous peoples|Indigenous peoples]] are renowned for their basket-weaving techniques.

Team sport in which two teams of five players each score by shooting a ball through a hoop at each end of a rectangular court. A field goal is worth two points, or three when made from behind the three-point line, and the team with the most points wins. Players advance the ball by dribbling or passing. Invented in 1891 by Canadian-American gym teacher James Naismith in Springfield, Massachusetts, the sport has become one of the world's most popular. The [[National Basketball Association]] (NBA) is the most significant professional league in terms of popularity, salaries, talent and level of competition. Top clubs from national leagues qualify for continental championships such as the [[EuroLeague]]. The WNBA is the main North American women's professional league.

Species of [[Shark|shark]] (*Cetorhinus maximus*), the second-largest living fish after the [[Whale shark]]. Basking sharks typically reach 7.9 m (26 ft) in length, and some grow more than 10 m (33 ft). A slow-moving filter feeder, it feeds at the surface, which gives the species its common name. Found in all the world's temperate oceans, the basking shark is harmless to humans. Overexploitation for food, fins and liver oil has reduced its populations to the point where some have disappeared and others need protection.

Autonomous community of northern [[Spain]], also officially called Euskadi. It includes the Basque provinces of Álava (Araba), Biscay (Bizkaia) and Gipuzkoa (Guipúzcoa). With 2,242,343 inhabitants, it is the eighth most populous autonomous community in Spain. Vitoria-Gasteiz is the de facto capital, while [[Bilbao]] is the largest city by population. The Spanish Constitution of 1978 granted the Basque Country the status of nationality, but [[Basques|Basque]] nationalists argue that many Basques never endorsed the constitution, pointing to the region's high abstention in its referendum. The Statute of Autonomy was approved in a referendum held on October 25, 1979. The Economist has described the region as having more autonomy than just about any other in Europe.

Language of the [[Basques]], Europe's only known language isolate. Basque has 806,000 speakers, of whom 93.7% (756,000) are in the Spanish Basque Country and 6.3% (51,000) in France. Under [[Francisco Franco|Franco]]'s regime, Basque was suppressed in education and publishing, and newborns could not be registered under Basque names. A standardized form, *Euskara Batua*, was developed in the late 1960s. Basque grammar is agglutinative with ergative-absolutive alignment, markedly different from that of [[Indo-European languages]].
